transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Priya Nair (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Redwood Product), Marta Ruiz (OceanGuard VP ML), Samir Patel (Eng Manager), Lena Thompson (FinOps), Devon Park (SRE)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on per-path (route) usage analytics, cost decomposition, and how Redwood's Optimize recommendations and per-route dashboards can help OceanGuard reduce inference spend while keeping latency SLOs. Customer asked about VPC/private deployment, audit logs, and whether we can attribute cost to ML services vs user-facing inference. Next steps agreed: send pilot pricing, sandbox access, and request workload traces.

Topics covered:
- Per-route dashboards and route tagging
- Token-level cost breakdown and attribution to features
- Batching and KV cache tradeoffs for their multi-model flows
- Dedicated vs Hosted economics at different QPS
- Security: VPC, KMS, audit logs, retention

Action items called out during call:
- See action_items metadata above (Priya/Daniel/Marta/Lena)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Priya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I'll hand it to Marta to open, and Daniel will run the console walkthrough.
[00:12] Marta (OceanGuard): Hi, thanks, yeah we're excited. Wanted to see how you map usage back to our product paths, and whether we can spot the heavy hitters. We're trying to cut 20 to 30 percent off inference spend without increasing tail latency.
[00:25] Priya: Great, that's exactly the goal for today. Daniel, take it away.
[00:28] Daniel (Redwood SE): Cool. I'm going to share my screen — can everyone see the Redwood Console? (pause) Looks like yes. So this is the org view, and I pulled a 30-day window for OceanGuard sandbox traffic to show real patterns.
[00:45] Daniel: First thing I want to point out is the per-route summary up top — you can tag routes by product, by team, or by feature. For example, we mapped "payload-insight" and "litigation-flow" — sorry, bad example — but you get the idea.
[01:05] Samir (OceanGuard): Can you walk through the token breakdown? We bill per inference, but the heavy cost is the long-context summarizations.
[01:12] Daniel: Yep. Under the route view there is a token breakdown: prompt tokens, completion tokens, and model-specific multipliers. You'll see the cost per token plotted alongside 95th percentile latency.
[01:27] Daniel: You'll also see a column for cached hits — which is where the KV cache paid off for repeated prefixes. On this sample traffic, about 18% of completions hit the cache which cut per-token compute by roughly the same percent.
[01:40] Devon (OceanGuard): That cache number — is that on by default in Hosted? I thought cache required a private deployment.
[01:47] Alex (Redwood Product): Cache is available in all modes but the policies differ. Hosted has managed prefix caching with shared eviction heuristics; Dedicated and Private let you configure cache size and pin policies. The console surfaces which policy is active per route.
[02:05] Marta: And how confident are those cost numbers? We need them for finance forecasting.
[02:10] Priya: The console ties the token usage to our billing model — the 'cost' column is our internal per-token unit price multiplied by model profile (quantized variants, longer context costs more). For forecasting you can export the per-route CSV, or plug into the cost API.
[02:26] Lena (FinOps): Export's great. Do you do per-day breakdowns by user cohort? We need top consumers for chargeback.
[02:33] Daniel: Yes, you can pivot by user_id, team tag, or route. There's an anomalies view too, which surfaces sudden increases and attributes them to prompt shape changes or model rollouts.
[02:48] Samir: How does batching affect latency? Our user-facing latency SLO is 500ms p95. We don't want batching to blow past that.
[02:55] Daniel: Right — batching reduces cost but can add latency. The console shows simulated latency impact when enabling different batch sizes. For your 500ms p95 target, we recommended a small batch size for chat routes and larger batches for background scoring jobs. We also surface adaptive batching recommendations based on your QPS shape.
[03:15] Marta: Can we see an example for one of our heavy routes?
[03:18] Daniel: Sure — I'm switching to the route detail for "agent-brief" which in our sample is the heavy hitter.
[03:25] [03:25] Daniel: Here you can see average tokens per request at the top, total calls, and the cost per thousand requests. Note the spike mid-month — that's when the team rolled a longer system prompt. The console shows the diff and you can link to the commit message if you connect your CI.
[03:45] Priya: That commit-linking is optional but popular — it helps tie cost regressions to product changes.
[03:50] Samir: That spike — can you break down why costs grew? Model change? Longer prompts? More users?
[03:54] Daniel: The decomposition view shows it's mostly increased average completion length — prompt stayed same but average completion tokens jumped ~40%. There's a small bump in traffic too.
[04:05] Lena: For our finance team I'd like a per-feature cost report monthly. Is that automated?
[04:09] Daniel: Yes, you can create scheduled reports and deliver to S3 or email. The PDF/CSV includes per-route, per-team, and per-user buckets.
[04:17] Marta: Security — we need audit logs with user actions and model changes for SOC2. How granular are your logs?
[04:24] Daniel: We record token-level usage, API keys, route changes, deployments, who triggered rollbacks — retention is configurable. For Private deployments logs can be routed through your SIEM.
[04:34] Devon: If we run private, do we still get the Console UI hosted, or do you give us a control plane?
[04:40] Alex: For Private you get a customer-managed control plane option — either a hosted console that connects into your VPC over private peering, or a self-hosted console bundle. We usually discuss on contract which approach fits compliance requirements.
[04:56] Marta: Pricing question — you said different model variants alter unit cost. If we quantize a model, how does quality degrade and how do we detect it?
[05:04] Daniel: We include Evaluate sets in Optimize. You can run a prompt suite pre/post quantization and get mismatch rates, BLEU-like scores, or custom business metrics. The console flags regressions and can rollback traffic to the higher fidelity variant automatically.
[05:23] Samir: That auto-rollback — is it instant? What triggers it?
[05:27] Daniel: You set thresholds for quality delta or user-facing errors. When thresholds are hit the router will divert traffic; depending on configuration failover is immediate to the stable variant.
[05:36] Lena: Are we able to set cost caps at route level so that an unbounded experiment doesn't blow our budget?
[05:42] Daniel: Yes — there are per-route spend limits and circuit-breakers. You can set daily spend caps, token caps, or QPS caps; the router will reject or redirect requests when limits are reached.
[05:53] Marta: Let's talk about a realistic pilot — we have three main flows: conversational support, batch classification, and long-context summarization. Which should we test first?
[06:03] Priya: From a cost/safety POV, batch classification is easiest — low latency tolerance and high QPS, good for cost optimization. Long-context summarization is the costliest; we can run Optimize recommendations on quantization and caching there.
[06:18] Samir: For long-context summarization, does KV cache help? Our prompts reuse the same user history a lot.
[06:23] Daniel: Yes, KV cache reduces compute for repeated prefixes. In the console we show cache hit rate by route. For your summarization route our sample showed 22% cache hit — we can tune policies to push that higher with some prompt engineering.
[06:36] Marta: Can we make cache invalidation deterministic for user privacy? We need to ensure PII is purged.
[06:42] Alex: You can set retention windows and explicit purge calls. If you're on Private we can plug into your KMS/HSM and lifecycle policies.
[06:51] Devon: On network egress — if we put Redwood in our VPC, does inference traffic leave our subnet?
[06:58] Daniel: If you choose Private or VPC peering, compute runs in your VPC or dedicated enclave. For Hosted there is encrypted transit and we provide contractual assurances; some customers with strict residency run Private.
[07:12] Samir: Can you demo the Optimize suggestions tab? We want to know concrete levers we'd get.
[07:17] Daniel: Switching over — Optimize suggests three levers: batching, quantization variant, and route-level caching flags. For each lever we show estimated cost delta and projected latency impact.
[07:31] Daniel: For example, for the "agent-brief" route, quantizing to int8 gives an estimated 32% lower cost but increases median latency ~10ms; adaptive batching at observed QPS reduces token cost another 8%.
[07:44] Marta: Those are estimates — how accurate are they?
[07:47] Daniel: Estimates are model-profile driven and derived from benchmark kernels on similar hardware. We attach a confidence band; when you run a pilot on your actual traces we produce empirical numbers.
[07:59] Priya: We usually recommend a two-week sandbox run with one or two routes to get real data. That will let us produce a firm proposition for Dedicated or Hosted.
[08:10] Lena: On the billing side, will the invoice show per-route breakdown? We need that for chargeback to product teams.
[08:16] Priya: Yes — invoices can include line items per route or per-project depending on your tagging; we also provide a billing export you can ingest into your finance system.
[08:26] Samir: For the sandbox pilot — how much effort to onboard? We run k8s in EKS and use our own model registry.
[08:34] Daniel: Minimal. You can either forward traffic through our SDK/clients or proxy with our gateway. We'll give you sample route YAMLs; Dedicated has a couple extra infra steps. Daniel: (muttering) I'll attach the quickstart we usually send.
[08:49] Marta: A security person asked whether API keys can be scoped to routes and rotated automatically.
[08:53] Alex: Keys are mappable to roles and restricted to routes/projects; we also support short-lived tokens and rotation hooks integrated with common secret managers.
[09:03] Devon: For SREs, we'd like to set alerts when token spend jumps 2x day-over-day. Can we create those in the console?
[09:09] Daniel: Absolutely — threshold alerts and anomaly detection can notify via Slack, PagerDuty, or email and include a link to the suspicious trace set.
[09:18] Samir: About the commit linking — if we hook up GitHub, will the console show which PR caused the cost change?
[09:23] Daniel: Yes — if you enable the integration and annotate deploys, the console will show correlated commits. It won't be perfect but it surfaces likely culprits.
[09:35] Lena: Do you offer a sandbox cost estimate generator? For procurement we need an expected spend for pilot variants.
[09:42] Priya: We do — I'll generate a pilot estimate based on the three flows you mentioned and provide both Hosted and Dedicated comparatives.
[09:52] Marta: Can you show a quick example of a scheduled report?
[09:55] Daniel: Sure — creating a scheduled report is just a few clicks. I'm setting up a weekly CSV for "agent-brief" per-route cost and user tag breakdown, sending to an S3 bucket. (typing noises) There we go — sample report ready.
[10:12] Marta: Nice. Will the CSV include token-level resolution?
[10:15] Daniel: You can choose granularity: request, hourly, or per-token aggregates. For most finance workflows hourly aggregates are sufficient.
[10:23] Devon: What about performance telemetry e.g., GPU utilization per model, or kernel-level breakdown?
[10:30] Alex: For Dedicated we surface HW telemetry including GPU util, memory, and per-worker queue length. For Hosted we show aggregate latency and per-variant metrics but not raw GPU counters.
[10:44] Samir: We use two models — a llama-style open model and a smaller encoder-only for embeddings. Can you host multiple models and route traffic by intent?
[10:52] Daniel: Yes, routing policies let you send a percent of traffic to different model variants for canarying. You can route by route, header, or confidence thresholds.
[11:02] Priya: Quick question — are there any third-party costs we should be aware of? Like cloud egress or special storage?
[11:08] Alex: If you run Dedicated in our hosted region we include compute and local storage. Egress to other regions or cross-cloud transfers incur cloud charges; that's surfaced in the cost export.
[11:20] Marta: Any gotchas with long-context models and memory pressure?
[11:24] Daniel: Long contexts increase KV cache and memory usage; quantization helps but not all kernels benefit equally. The console flags routes that are memory-intensive and suggests splitting or streaming.
[11:35] Samir: OK, I'd like to see a sample workflow: we pick one route, run a two-week sandbox, apply Optimize suggestions, then decide Dedicated or Hosted. How long to set up once we approve?
[11:46] Priya: For Hosted pilot you can be live within a day with our SDK and a sample YAML. For Dedicated, onboarding is typically 2–4 weeks depending on capacity and security review.
[11:56] Lena: SLA question — what uptime/latency SLAs do you offer on Dedicated?
[12:00] Priya: Dedicated gets tighter SLAs including a commitment on p95 latency and a higher uptime SLA; exact numbers are contract dependent. We'll include the SLA matrix in the follow-up.
[12:12] Marta: Can you show a quick example of an anomaly alert drilling into traces?
[12:16] Daniel: Switching to anomalies view — here's a spike flagged as a latency anomaly. I can click into the sample traces and see the prompt shapes, the model variant and the worker that served it. Sometimes you'll see a single bad prompt skewing p95.
[12:35] Devon: What's the false-positive rate on anomaly detection?
[12:38] Daniel: It depends on volume and thresholds — we tune for low-noise alerts for higher QPS routes. We also allow manual suppression windows.
[12:48] Marta: Let's talk about contract triggers — if we hit a cost threshold, is there a process to pause or throttle?
[12:54] Priya: Yes, we can implement contractual guardrails; the console-level caps provide operational control and we can add billing alerts tied to thresholds.
[13:07] Samir: One last technical: can we run in an air-gapped environment for regulated customers?
[13:12] Alex: We offer an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments. It's heavier lift but doable; it includes the private control plane and audit log exports.
[13:23] Marta: Great. Anything else from the Redwood side?
[13:26] Priya: I want to highlight the pilot proposal — we'll include concrete cost estimates, expected savings with Optimize, and an onboarding checklist. Daniel will provision sandbox and Alex will attach security docs.
[13:37] Marta: That's good. For the pilot, we'll aim to start the first week of December.
[13:41] Priya: Sounds good. We'll get the materials to you by early next week.
[13:45] Samir: Quick nit — can you include an example of per-route SLA objectives in the documentation? I'd like engineering to see how they map to router config.
[13:52] Daniel: Yes, I'll include example route YAMLs with SLO fields and circuit-breaker config.
[13:58] Lena: And please include an example invoice showing per-route line items for the pilot.
[14:03] Priya: Will do.
[14:07] Marta: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[14:10] Devon: Thanks.
[14:11] Alex: Thanks team, we'll follow up.

[14:20] End of recording.
